data_schema.title: USDA Directive Extraction Schema v2.1 (DR/DM)
data_schema.description: Extracts metadata and structured policy statements from 3000 series USDA Departmental Regulation (DR) or Departmental Manual (DM). Governing rules: (1) Any field described as verbatim must be copied character-for-character from the source document. Never paraphrase, merge, abbreviate, summarize, or insert ellipses. (2) Do not infer. If the source does not support an optional field, leave the field out entirely. Never return an empty string or a guess. (3) Only the label fields in policy_statements (statement_kind, statement_function, modal_use, normative_force, actor_basis) are interpretations. Every other field is quoted or copied from the document.

document_type.description: Type of document as printed in the header, such as 'Departmental Regulation' or 'Departmental Manual'.

issuing_organization.description: Organization issuing the document, verbatim from the header.

issuing_location.description: Location of the issuing organization, verbatim from the header.

regulation_number.description: Official document number from the header, verbatim, for example 'DR 3105-001'.

subject.description: Subject or title of the document, verbatim from the header.

issue_date.description: Issue date from the header, as written.

expiration_date.description: Expiration date from the header, as written. Leave out if none is printed.

opi.description: Office of Primary Interest (OPI) from the header, verbatim.

supersedes.description: The prior document this document supersedes. Take all values from the supersession paragraph in the body (usually under Special Instructions/Cancellations), NOT from the header. Leave the whole object out if the document supersedes nothing.

document_number.description: Number of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph. If it is identical to this document's own number, still copy it from the supersession paragraph, not the header.

document_title.description: Title of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph.

document_date.description: Date of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph.

scope.description: The text of the Scope section, verbatim. Do not add words. Leave out if the document has no Scope section.

purpose.description: The text of the Purpose section, verbatim. Do not add words. Leave out if the document has no Purpose section.

inquiries.description: Contact information from the Inquiries section. Leave out any property the document does not state; never return an empty string.

office.description: Office or division named for inquiries, verbatim. Leave out if the document names no office.

email.description: Email address given for inquiries, verbatim, without trailing punctuation. Leave out if none is given.

table_of_contents.description: Top-level entries of the printed table of contents, in order, including appendices. Return an empty list if the document prints no table of contents.

section_number.description: Section or appendix identifier as printed, for example '1.' or 'Appendix A'.

section_title.description: Section or appendix title as printed in the table of contents.

page.description: Page number exactly as printed in the table of contents, for example '2' or 'A-1'. Copy it even if the section actually starts on a different page. Leave out if no page number is printed.

actors.description: Registry of every distinct entity that the policy text names in an acting role. One entry per entity. Include every entity used as actor_name in policy_statements. Also include entities the document names in a role without being directed to act (mark those mentioned_only). Documents (bylaws, regulations, directives) are NEVER actors and must not appear here. Return an empty list if the document names no actors.

name.description: The entity's name exactly as written in the policy text, without a leading article ('the') and without a possessive. Keep a compound name intact if the document writes it as one phrase, for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices'. This is the join key used by actor_name in policy_statements, so spell it identically there.

components.description: ONLY for a name that joins separate entities with commas or 'and' (for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices' gives 'USDA Mission Areas', 'agencies', 'staff offices'). NEVER split a job title from the organization that qualifies it ('Director of IT, Office of the Inspector General' is ONE position), and never split an organization name from the position it modifies ('Office of the Chief Information Officer (OCIO) Associate CIOs (ACIO)' is ONE group). Each component is a verbatim substring of the name. Leave out for single entities.

items.description: One verbatim component of a compound actor name.

actor_type.description: Kind of entity. Use exactly one of: position (a job title, singular or plural, for example 'USDA CIO' or 'Mission Area Assistant CIOs'), office (an organizational unit, for example 'OCIO Executive Secretariat'), council_or_body (a council, committee, board, or similar body), group (a category of organizations or units, not job titles, for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices'), external_entity (an entity outside the document's authority), program_or_system (an IT initiative, system, program, or project that the document says must act or conform).

binding_status.description: bound_by_this_document: the document directs, permits, or assigns a function or role to this entity and has authority over it. mentioned_only: the document names the entity but cannot or does not impose anything on it (for example a council or agency outside USDA that the document says a USDA body partners with).

policy_statements.description: Structured statements from the numbered body sections only (not the table of contents, not the appendices). RULES. (a) SENTENCES: emit one statement per sentence. If a paragraph has more than one sentence, give each its own statement with ids suffixed .s1, .s2, and so on. Abbreviations and legal citations ('U.S.C.', 'CFR', '§', 'et seq.') do not end a sentence. (b) LISTS: when text introduces a list (usually ends with a colon, for example 'The USDA CIO will:'), emit the introducing text as one statement with statement_kind 'lead_in', and emit EVERY item of the list as its own statement with statement_kind 'list_item' and parent_statement_id set to the id of the lead_in. Never skip list items, including lists of legal authorities. For a list inside a list, parent_statement_id is the immediate parent. (c) NEVER merge text from different sentences, paragraphs, or list items into one statement. (d) Copy text exactly; do not summarize. (e) PRONOUNS: when a sentence's subject is a pronoun ('It', 'Its', 'They') that refers to a named actor in the preceding sentence, resolve it: set actor_name to that actor and actor_basis to resolved_from_prior_sentence. (f) DOCUMENT AS SUBJECT: when the grammatical subject is the document itself ('This DR', 'This policy', 'Nothing in this DR'), leave actor_name out; the entities the document acts on belong in target.

statement_id.description: Printed numbering path of the statement: section number, then paragraph letter, then item number in parentheses, for example '1', '3.a', '5.d.s2', '6.a(1)'. Add '.sN' only when a paragraph contains more than one sentence. Must be unique within the document.

statement_kind.description: standalone: a complete sentence that stands on its own. lead_in: text that introduces a list and is incomplete without its items. list_item: a list item that completes its lead_in.

parent_statement_id.description: Include ONLY when statement_kind is list_item: the statement_id of its immediate lead_in. For every other statement leave this field out entirely; never return an empty string.

section_number.description: Number of the section containing the statement, digits only, for example '6'.

section_title.description: Title of the section containing the statement, as shown in the table of contents, for example 'Roles and Responsibilities'.

source_text.description: VERBATIM text of this one sentence or list item exactly as printed, including trailing punctuation such as ':' or ';' and including any list-ending words such as 'and'. No paraphrase, no ellipses, no text from any other statement. For a list_item, give only the item's own text, not the lead_in.

statement_function.description: What the statement does. obligation: a required action or compliance requirement on an actor. responsibility: a standing duty or function assigned to an actor, including present-tense descriptions of what a body does. role_designation: assigns an entity to a role, for example membership or voting status. authority: names a legal source of authority or a grant of authority. scope: states what or whom the document applies to. purpose: states why the document or a body exists. definition: defines a term. condition: states a standalone triggering condition. exception: carves out an exception. savings_clause: states that the document does not displace existing authorities or delegations. effectivity: states when the document takes effect or how long it lasts. supersession: states that the document replaces another. classification_rule: states a rule that classifies something or applies a requirement when a status is met. reference: points to another document or location. inquiry: tells who may be contacted. container: use for every lead_in statement. other: none of the above.

modal_verb.description: The modal word or phrase of the statement's MAIN clause, exactly as written, for example 'will', 'can', 'may', 'must', 'shall', 'must not'. Ignore modals inside relative or subordinate clauses (for 'advises the USDA CIO on IT matters that may become IT investments', the 'may' is not the statement's modal). For a list_item whose own text has no modal, copy the modal from its lead_in. Leave out if the main clause has no modal.

modal_use.description: deontic: the main-clause modal directs, permits, or prohibits action by an actor (for example 'The Deputy CIO will serve', 'can direct questions'). predictive: the modal only states what will happen or remain true (for example 'It will remain in effect until superseded'). none: the main clause has no modal.

normative_force.description: mandatory: deontic 'will', 'shall', or 'must' directing an actor to act or to serve in a role. prohibitive: deontic 'must not', 'shall not', or 'may not'. permissive: deontic 'may' or 'can'. assigned: a present-tense statement with no deontic modal that assigns or describes a function, duty, or role of a named actor (for example 'The CIO Council advises the USDA CIO on...', 'It assesses the needs of...'); use it only when actor_name is present, and never for purpose statements. descriptive: everything else with no deontic force, including purpose, scope, supersession, effectivity, savings clauses, references, authorities, definitions, and statements about the document itself or about other documents. not_applicable: use for every lead_in; its force is carried by its list_items.

actor_name.description: The entity directed to act, permitted to act, or assigned a function or role by this statement, spelled exactly as in the matching actors[].name. It must appear in source_text or in the lead_in's text (leading article removed); for a resolved pronoun, copy it from the antecedent sentence. Leave out when the statement binds no actor: scope, supersession, effectivity, savings clauses, statements about documents (including bylaws), and any statement whose subject is the document itself ('This DR', 'This policy', 'Nothing in this DR'). Never supply an actor that is not stated in the text or resolvable from the preceding sentence. Always leave out for lead_in statements.

actor_basis.description: Include ONLY when actor_name is present; otherwise leave this field out entirely. explicit_in_statement: the actor appears in this statement's own source_text. inherited_from_lead_in: the actor appears only in the lead_in that this list_item completes. resolved_from_prior_sentence: the subject is a pronoun resolved to the actor named in the preceding sentence.

target.description: VERBATIM phrase naming what the action is directed at or what the statement applies to, starting at the first word after any leading article ('a', 'an', 'the'). For a role_designation, the body or unit the role is within (for example 'CIO Council'). Leave out if none.

resulting_status.description: VERBATIM phrase naming the status or role that a role_designation or classification_rule confers, for example 'voting member' or 'advisory (non-voting) members'. Leave out for other statements.

conditions.description: VERBATIM phrases that restrict when or to what the statement applies, for example 'that the CIO Council designates as enterprise initiatives'. Do NOT treat a non-restrictive descriptive phrase set off by commas (for example 'appointed by the USDA CIO' in 'The Secretariat, appointed by the USDA CIO, will serve') as a condition. Leave out if there are none.

items.description: One verbatim condition phrase copied from source_text.

cross_references.description: Other documents, laws, or regulations cited in source_text, each copied verbatim as ONE entry per cited authority, including its code citation (for example 'The Clinger-Cohen Act of 1996, 40 United States Code (U.S.C.) § 11101 et seq.' is one entry; for a list_item that is just a citation, the entry is the item text without the trailing ';' or 'and'). Never add a separate entry for a title that is part of the same citation (the words 'Chief Information Officer' after '7 CFR § 2.32'). Never list generic categories such as 'law' or 'Federal regulation'. Leave out if none.

acronyms.description: Acronyms and abbreviations listed in the acronym appendix, one entry per row, in order. Return an empty list if the document has no acronym appendix.

acronym.description: Acronym or abbreviation exactly as printed.

authorities_and_references.description: Entries of the Authorities and References appendix, one per entry, each copied verbatim, including any date, in order. Return an empty list if the document has no such appendix.

items.description: One appendix entry exactly as printed, joined across line breaks.

policy_statements.source_text: This Departmental Manual (DM) establishes the processes required for determining which standards (technical, data, and hybrid (technical/data)) to use for the acquisition, configuration, and administration of information technology (IT) within the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA).
This DM provides the procedures necessary to apply Departmental Regulation (DR) DR 3180-001, Information Technology Standards, throughout USDA.
cross_references: Departmental Regulation (DR) DR 3180-001, Information Technology Standards

policy_statements.source_text: DR 3180-001 supports and implements the guidance issued by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the Federal Information Technology Acquisition Reform Act (FITARA), Public Law (P.L.) 113-291 Sections 831-837, and other Federal oversight entities.
cross_references: Federal Information Technology Acquisition Reform Act (FITARA), Public Law (P.L.) 113-291 Sections 831-837

policy_statements.source_text: It facilitates the uniform application of engineering and/or technical criteria, methods, processes, and practices when evaluating and procuring new technologies; ensures new technologies align with USDA enterprise architecture (EA), business goals, and processes; and meets the requirements of the following policy documents:
OMB, Circular A-130, Managing Information as a Strategic Resource; and
cross_references: OMB, Circular A-130, Managing Information as a Strategic Resource

policy_statements.source_text: OMB, Circular A-119, Federal Participation in the Development and Use of Voluntary Consensus Standards and in Conformity Assessment Activities.
cross_references: OMB, Circular A-119, Federal Participation in the Development and Use of Voluntary Consensus Standards and in Conformity Assessment Activities

policy_statements.source_text: The benefits of standardization to all users within USDA include:
Providing cost avoidance and improved integration through elimination or consolidation of duplicative processes, systems, and/or technologies;
Ensuring acquisition and use of standard information technologies and/or cloud services;
Ensuring correctness, completeness, and currency of the standard profiles through the definition of roles, responsibilities, and processes;
Enhancing interoperability (data, security, technology) between programs, systems, and services; and
Improving consistency, accuracy, and timeliness of information shared across the USDA enterprise.
This DM supports DR 3180-001 and applies to all USDA Mission Areas, agencies, staff offices, employees, and contractors working for, or on behalf of, USDA.
policy_statements.target: USDA Mission Areas, agencies, staff offices, employees, and contractors working for, or on behalf of, USDA

policy_statements.source_text: Use this DM in conjunction with DR 3180-001.
The term “agency” or phrase “agency and staff office,” unless otherwise noted in this document, will be considered to encompass the Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices of USDA.
conditions: unless otherwise noted in this document

policy_statements.source_text: The Clinger-Cohen Act of 1996, 40 United States Code (U.S.C.) Section 11101 et seq. (2017) was enacted to improve the way the Federal Government acquires, uses, and disposes of IT.
cross_references: Clinger-Cohen Act of 1996, 40 United States Code (U.S.C.) Section 11101 et seq. (2017)

policy_statements.source_text: The E-Government Act of 2002, Public Law (P.L.) 107-347 (codified at various sections of Title 44, Chapters 35 and 36) drives the design and development of an EA within Federal Agencies.
cross_references: E-Government Act of 2002, Public Law (P.L.) 107-347 (codified at various sections of Title 44, Chapters 35 and 36)

policy_statements.source_text: Circular A-119 requires Federal Agencies to use voluntary consensus standards in lieu of unique Government standards, with the intention of reducing to a minimum the reliance by Agencies on unique Government standards.
policy_statements.actor_name: Federal Agencies

policy_statements.source_text: The following are examples of voluntary consensus standards bodies: International Organization for Standardization (ISO), Federal Geographic Data Committee (FGDC), National Information Exchange Model (NIEM), and World Wide Web Consortium (W3C).

IT standards are rules or specifications designed to simplify, unify, or rationalize the design, interoperability, portability, and scalability of IT infrastructure components (e.g., network, hardware, systems, cloud services, and software).

FITARA requires that the Department’s Chief Information Officer (CIO) coordinate FITARA-related activities with other senior Department officials including: the Chief Financial Officer (CFO), the Chief Acquisition Officer (CAO), the Chief Operating Officer (COO, the Deputy Secretary; represented by the USDA Assistant Secretary for Administration, the Senior Procurement Executive (SPE), the Chief Human Capital Officer (CHCO), and the Director of the Office of Budget and Program Analysis (OBPA).
policy_statements.actor_name: Department’s Chief Information Officer (CIO)

policy_statements.source_text: The USDA CIO, CFO, COO, CAO, SPE, CHCO, and OBPA Director, as a group, identify as the Chief Executive Officers (CXO).
policy_statements.actor_name: USDA CIO, CFO, COO, CAO, SPE, CHCO, and OBPA Director

policy_statements.source_text: The CXOs tasks include fully defining and understanding the costs of Mission Area, agency, and staff office IT investments, products, and services be incorporated into the USDA budget formulation, budget execution, acquisition, and IT workforce-planning processes.
policy_statements.actor_name: CXOs
policy_statements.target: costs of Mission Area, agency, and staff office IT investments, products, and services

policy_statements.source_text: DR 3185-001, Enterprise Architecture, states, “A documented and understood EA provides a framework for the organization to respond quickly to changes in its operating environment.

It serves as a ready reference that enables the organization to assess the impact of the changes on each of the six EA components (business, data, infrastructure, technology, applications, and security), as well as ensuring the components continue to operate smoothly through the changes.”
The Technical Standards Profile is part of the Infrastructure domain.

The Common Approach to Federal Enterprise Architecture (Common Approach) presents an overall approach to developing and using EA in the Federal Government by promoting increased levels of mission effectiveness by standardizing the development and use of architectures within and between Federal Agencies.
cross_references: The Common Approach to Federal Enterprise Architecture (Common Approach)

policy_statements.source_text: Within the Common Approach, in the Infrastructure Domain, the I-3, Technical Standards Profile is the artifact that captures the relevant standards that are in support of the systems that the Mission Area, agency, or staff office maintains.

Related implementation guidance from the OMB is contained in various documents, including Circulars A-11, Preparation, Submission, and Execution of the Budget; A-130; OMB, Memoranda M-00-10, OMB Procedures and Guidance on Implementing the Government Paperwork Elimination Act; M-05-22, Transition Planning for Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6); M-11-29, Chief Information Officer Authorities; M-12-10, Implementing PortfolioStat; and the Digital Government: Building a 21st Century Platform to Better Serve The American People.
cross_references: Circulars A-11, Preparation, Submission, and Execution of the Budget
OMB, Memoranda M-00-10, OMB Procedures and Guidance on Implementing the Government Paperwork Elimination Act
M-05-22, Transition Planning for Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6)
Digital Government: Building a 21st Century Platform to Better Serve The American People

policy_statements.source_text: The Federal Enterprise Architecture Framework, v 2.0 (FEAF v2) is the suite of tools to help Government planners implement the Common Approach.
cross_references: Federal Enterprise Architecture Framework, v 2.0 (FEAF v2)

policy_statements.source_text: Identification of standards for systems relies on the business, functional, and technical requirements of the system as determined by the system owners/stakeholders.
Business, functional, and technical requirements will help to identify standards for a system.
Business requirements, which are not technical in nature, focus on fulfilling Mission Area, agency, and staff office needs or business goals.
Functional requirements are technical and provide detailed information about how a software system functions.
Business requirements for a project are a series of needs that achieve a high-level objective.
Business requirements describe the customers’ needs.
They clearly state Mission Area, agency, and staff office objectives and prioritize the problems Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices need to solve.
These documents do more than just narrate the needs and solutions.
They may contain diagrams, organizational charts, and flowcharts.
Functional requirements describe how a software system functions.
They delve into how users interact with the software, such as what actions occur after users click on buttons and show the outcome of these actions.
Functional requirements also show how other databases or software applications integrate with each other.
They specify the hardware and operating system requirements that the software system will be using.

Functional requirements are a detailed breakdown that explains how the outcome of a project will operate to meet the specified business requirements that address a specific need or pain point identified by the end user or stakeholder.
Technical requirements establish what a Mission Area, agency, or staff office needs to do to support the project’s outcome during and after implementation.
The standards profile defines the technical, operational, business, policy, and guidance standards applicable to the architecture.
In addition to identifying applicable technical standards, the standards profile also documents the policies and standards that apply to the operational or business context.
In most cases, building a standards profile consists of identifying and listing the applicable portions of existing and emerging documentation.
A Standards Profile should identify both existing guidelines, as well as any areas lacking guidance.
As with other models, each profile is assigned a specific timescale (e.g., as-is, to-be, or transitional).

Linking the profile to a defined timescale enables the enterprise architect to consider both emerging technologies and any current technical standards that are being updated (becoming mature) or becoming obsolete (to be retired).

The standards profile collates and delineates the various systems and services, standards, and rules that implement and constrain the choices in the design and implementation of an architectural description.
The technical standards govern what hardware and software may be implemented and on what system.
The standards cited may be international (such as ISO standards), national standards, or organizational specific standards.
With associated standards, as with other elements of the architecture, a distinction between applicability and conformance.
If a standard is applicable to a given architecture, that architecture need not fully conform with the standard.
conditions: If a standard is applicable to a given architecture

policy_statements.source_text: The degree of conformance to a given standard is based on a risk assessment at each approval point.

Note that an association between a standard and an architectural element does not indicate that the element is fully compliant with that standard; rather further detail would need to confirm the level of compliance.
Standards profiles for an architectural design must maintain full compatibility with the root standards.
Furthermore, the standards profile model may state a method of implementation for a standard, as compliance with a standard does not ensure interoperability.
The standards forecast contains expected changes in technical, operational, business, guidance, and policy standards and conventions documented in the standards profile.
A standards forecast is a detailed description of emerging standards relevant to the systems, operational, and business activities covered by the Architectural Description.
The forecast focuses on areas that relate to the purpose for which a given architectural description should identify issues that affect the architecture.
A standards forecast complements and expands on the standards profile and should be used when more than one emerging standard period is applicable to the architecture.
conditions: when more than one emerging standard period is applicable to the architecture

policy_statements.source_text: One of the prime purposes of a standards forecast is to identify critical technology standards, their fragility, and the impact of these standards on the future development and maintainability of the architecture and its constituent elements.
The standards forecast contains expected changes in standards and conventions, documented in the standards profile.

One of the prime purposes of a standards forecast is to identify critical standards, their life expectancy, and the impact of these standards on the future development and maintainability of the architectural description and its constituent elements.
A Standards forecast lists emerging or evolving standards relevant to the solutions covered by the architectural description.
Ensure that the specific periods selected (e.g., 6-month, 18-month, 36-month intervals) and the standards being tracked are coordinated with architecture transition plans.
That is, inserting new capabilities and upgrading existing solutions may depend on the availability of new standards and models incorporating those standards.
The forecast specifies potential standards, thus influences current architectures and influences the development of transition and objective (i.e., target) architectures.
The forecast focuses on standards/service areas that relate to the purpose for which a given architecture design described and should identify potential standards affecting that architecture.
The standards forecast delineates the standards that potentially affect the relevant system and service elements and relates them to the periods.
A system’s evolution, or service’s evolutions, ties to a future standard listed in the standards forecast.

A timed technology and skills forecast relates to the standards forecast in the following manner: a certain technology may depend on a standards forecast standard (i.e., a standard listed in the standards forecast may not be adopted until a certain technology becomes available).
This is how a prediction on the adoption of a future standard may be related to standards listed in the standards profile.
Mission Area, agency, and staff office Enterprise Architects shall adhere to the following procedures when determining relevant standards for their respective systems profiles and forecasts:
conditions: when determining relevant standards for their respective systems profiles and forecasts

policy_statements.source_text: Establish uniform engineering and technical criteria;

Manage the replacement of systems, applications, hardware, software, and other technologies that are in alignment with the current in-force standards; and

policy_statements.source_text: Construct technical system standards profiles and forecasts using the following procedure/steps:
Determine the specific need or pain point based on requirements that need to be addressed:
Systems do not exist that could address the needs of the stakeholder.
Are there current systems not meeting needs of the customer/stakeholder?
The customer/stakeholder identifies requirements that a Mission Area, agency, or staff office needs to ensure mission completeness.
policy_statements.actor_name: customer/stakeholder
policy_statements.target: requirements that a Mission Area, agency, or staff office needs to ensure mission completeness

policy_statements.source_text: Identify business, functional, and technical requirements for system(s) to address the need/pain point experienced by the stakeholder/customer:
Determine the business, functional, and technical requirements that currently exist or need to be developed.
policy_statements.target: business, functional, and technical requirements that currently exist or need to be developed

policy_statements.source_text: Identify and capture requirements based on information gathering with the stakeholders.
Discuss with the development staff the requirements obtained from the stakeholder and determine if a current system needs enhancement or if a new system needs development.
Determine if there is an existing, approved capability that will satisfy the new requirements:
Is there a known shared service that can be used to address the need/pain point identified by another Mission Area, agency, or staff office?
Will the identified system interoperate with the current Mission Area, agency, or staff office’s system or application?
Is there an existing standards profile/forecast?
Provide standards profile/forecast to shared site.
Profiles/forecasts should reflect ability to address the current system or application requirements.
Profiles/forecasts should also incorporate identified requirements.
If no system/shared service exists:
Consult with the Enterprise Architecture Division (EAD) to determine if there is an approved platform standard for the business need.
If not, conduct an analysis of alternatives (AOA) and identify recommended solution (s) (to include systems and subsystems); and
Use identified requirements to:
Identify standards to address system requirements to operate within the Mission Area, agency, and staff office environment; and
Use a standards forecast to identify the future state once a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) or Government off-the-shelf (GOTS) product is identified.
conditions: once a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) or Government off-the-shelf (GOTS) product is identified

policy_statements.source_text: A Determination needs to be made:
Is the product a COTS or customized GOTS system/subsystem?
If COTS, ensure that the vendor is compliant with a baseline standards profile, identified in DR 3180-001, to operate within the Mission Area, agency, and staff office network; and
If GOTS, ensure that the development staff works with the entities that can identify current and in-force standards as identified in DR 3180-001.

Circular A-119 requires Federal Agencies to use voluntary consensus standards in lieu of unique Government standards, with the intention of reducing to a minimum the reliance by Agencies on unique Government standards.

Business, functional, and technical requirements will help to identify standards for a system.
Business requirements, which are not technical in nature, focus on fulfilling Mission Area, agency, and staff office needs or business goals.
Functional requirements are technical and provide detailed information about how a software system functions.
Business requirements for a project are a series of needs that achieve a high-level objective.
Business requirements describe the customers’ needs.
They clearly state Mission Area, agency, and staff office objectives and prioritize the problems Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices need to solve.
These documents do more than just narrate the needs and solutions.
They may contain diagrams, organizational charts, and flowcharts.
Functional requirements describe how a software system functions.
They delve into how users interact with the software, such as what actions occur after users click on buttons and show the outcome of these actions.
Functional requirements also show how other databases or software applications integrate with each other.
They specify the hardware and operating system requirements that the software system will be using.

Functional requirements are a detailed breakdown that explains how the outcome of a project will operate to meet the specified business requirements that address a specific need or pain point identified by the end user or stakeholder.
Technical requirements establish what a Mission Area, agency, or staff office needs to do to support the project’s outcome during and after implementation.
